nameStory: Pacific golden dock gets its name from its golden-yellow flower clusters and its origin along the Pacific coast of North America. The 'dock' part comes from an old English word for these sturdy plants with their characteristic broad leaves, while 'golden' refers to the bright yellow blooms that catch the eye in summer.
description: Pacific golden dock is a rare visitor to New England, an annual herb that typically grows 1-3 feet tall with narrow, lance-shaped leaves. This member of the knotweed family produces clusters of tiny golden-yellow flowers in summer that later develop into small, three-sided fruits. It's a western North American native that occasionally shows up in our region, making it quite a special find for plant enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny golden-yellow flowers clustered in dense, branching spikes that feel papery when touched. The individual flowers are barely larger than a pinhead but create showy displays when massed together.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel smooth and slightly waxy to the touch. They're arranged alternately along the stem and often have a slight reddish tinge along the edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: An upright annual herb growing 1-3 feet tall with branching stems that feel firm but hollow when gently squeezed. The plant has a somewhat sparse, open appearance.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, three-sided brown fruits that develop from the flower clusters. They have a papery texture and make a subtle rattling sound when the dried seed heads are shaken.

habitat: Pacific golden dock is extremely rare in New England, with only three recorded observations in the region. When found, it typically grows in disturbed soils, roadsides, or waste areas where seeds may have arrived through long-distance transport. It prefers sunny, open locations with well-drained soil.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of narrow leaves, often going unnoticed among other weedy vegetation.
seasonality.summer: The plant reaches full height and produces its distinctive golden-yellow flower clusters, making this the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and develop into brown, three-sided fruits while leaves may turn reddish before the plant dies back.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, the plant dies completely, leaving only dried stems and scattered seeds that may persist into early winter.

funFact: This plant is so rare in New England that spotting one would be like finding botanical treasure - with only three confirmed sightings in the entire region, you'd be more likely to see a celebrity than this golden dock!
confusionNotes: Pacific golden dock could be confused with other dock species, but its golden-yellow flowers are distinctive - most other New England docks have greenish or reddish flowers. The narrow leaves also help separate it from broad-leaved dock and curled dock.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this species with the similarly named genus Persicaria (smartweeds) - despite the scientific name 'persicarioides' meaning 'resembling Persicaria,' this is definitely a true dock in the genus Rumex.
compareHints: Pacific golden dock stands out from other New England dock species primarily by its bright golden-yellow flowers - most relatives like curled dock and broad-leaved dock have greenish or reddish blooms. Its narrow leaves are more similar to willow dock than the broader-leaved species, but the flower color remains the key distinguishing feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its larger cousins the docks (broad-leaved dock, curled dock), sheep's sorrel stays much smaller and has those distinctive backward-pointing lobes on its leaves.

Among New England's dock species, broad-leaved dock is distinguished by its wide, flat-edged leaves – curled dock has wavy leaf margins, sheep's sorrel has arrow-shaped leaves, and swamp dock prefers wetland areas.
Among New England's dock species, curled dock is the easiest to identify thanks to its signature wavy leaf margins – no other dock has this feature.

Swamp dock differs from its dock relatives by its strong preference for wet habitats - while curled dock and broad-leaved dock are common weeds of dry disturbed soils, swamp dock sticks to marshes and wet areas.
Wood dock stands out dramatically from its dock relatives because of its red-veined leaves - no other dock species in New England has this feature.
Greater Water Dock stands apart from other New England docks by its wetland habitat and impressive size - it's notably larger than Curled Dock or Broad-leaved Dock.

Among the dock and sorrel family, common sorrel stands out with its distinctly arrow-shaped leaves and sour taste, while true docks like curled dock and broad-leaved dock have much larger, broader leaves without the pointed basal lobes and lack the sour flavor.
Northern dock stands out from other Rumex species by its long, narrow leaves with smooth edges - most other docks have broader leaves or wavy margins like curled dock.
Unlike its inland relatives like curled dock or broad-leaved dock, seabeach dock has much thicker, fleshier leaves and stays much lower to the ground.
White willow dock stands out from its dock relatives by having much narrower leaves - compare this to broad-leaved dock or curled dock which have wide, often wavy-edged leaves.
Among its dock relatives in New England, willow dock stands out with its narrow leaves - most other docks like broad-leaved dock and curled dock have much wider foliage.

Golden dock differs from other New England docks by its much smaller stature and distinctive golden flower clusters - most other docks like curled dock or broad-leaved dock are much larger perennial plants with reddish-brown flower clusters.
Golden dock stands out from its dock relatives by having much narrower leaves - more like a willow than the typical broad, paddle-shaped dock leaf.
Patience dock stands out from other New England docks by its exceptionally large size and smooth-edged leaves with heart-shaped bases.
